choices.text: One or more metals bound to one or more Lewis base ligands
A salt made only of simple metal cations and simple anions
choices.why: A coordination compound has ligands bound directly to the metal as Lewis bases, not just ions packed together.

choices.text: A molecule in which every atom contributes electrons to shared bonds
choices.why: That describes how ordinary molecules are usually pictured. In a complex, the ligand supplies the electron pair to the metal.

choices.text: A metal bound to one or more Lewis acid ligands
choices.why: Ligands are Lewis bases: they donate electron pairs. The metal is the Lewis acid.

explanation: Coordination compounds consist of one or more metals bound to one or more Lewis base ligands. In the hexaamminecobalt(3+) ion, for example, six ammonia ligands coordinate a Co^3+ ion.

prompt: In the coordinate covalent model of a metal–ligand bond, where do the two bonding electrons come from?

choices.text: Both come from the ligand
Both come from the metal
choices.why: In conventional complexes the metal is the acceptor. The ligand donates the pair.

choices.text: One comes from the metal and one from the ligand
choices.why: That is an ordinary covalent bond. In a coordinate covalent bond both electrons come from one partner, the ligand.

choices.text: They come from the counterions
choices.why: Counterions sit in the outer coordination sphere and don't supply the metal–ligand bonding pair.

explanation: The ligand–metal bond can be thought of as a coordinate covalent bond in which both bonding electrons come from the ligand, which is then said to coordinate the metal. The model is a useful formalism even where it doesn't capture every detail of the bonding.

prompt: In a conventional coordination compound, which roles do the ligand and the metal play?

choices.text: The ligand is the donor (Lewis base) and the metal is the acceptor (Lewis acid)
The metal is the donor (Lewis base) and the ligand is the acceptor (Lewis acid)
choices.why: This is reversed. The ligand donates its lone pair and the metal accepts it.

choices.text: Both are Lewis acids
choices.why: Something has to supply the electron pair. The ligand does, so it is a Lewis base.

choices.text: The counterion is the donor and the metal is the acceptor
choices.why: The donor is the ligand bound in the primary coordination sphere, not a counterion.

explanation: The portion that contributes the electron pair is the donor and the portion that receives it is the acceptor. In conventional coordination compounds the ligand is the donor (Lewis base) and the metal the acceptor (Lewis acid). Donor–acceptor language becomes handier in more complex bonding situations.

prompt: In [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, where are the three chloride ions?

choices.text: In the secondary (outer) coordination sphere, as counterions
In the primary (inner) coordination sphere, bound to cobalt
choices.why: Only what is inside the square brackets is in the primary sphere. Here that's the six NH3 ligands.

choices.text: Bonded to the nitrogen atoms of the ammonia ligands
choices.why: That was the old chain-theory picture. The chlorides are counterions outside the complex ion.

choices.text: Half inside and half outside the coordination sphere
choices.why: All three sit outside the brackets, so all three are in the outer sphere.

explanation: Ligands bound to the metal sit in the primary (inner) coordination sphere and aren't readily exchanged. Nearby counterions and solvent molecules are in the secondary (outer) sphere. In a formula, the square brackets enclose the primary sphere, so the three Cl^− outside [Co(NH3)6]^3+ are outer-sphere counterions.

prompt: What is the coordination number of cobalt in [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2?
explanation: The coordination number is the number of ligand sites donating lone pairs to the metal. The primary sphere is what's inside the brackets: five NH3 and one Cl^−, so 5 + 1 = 6. The two chlorides outside the brackets are counterions and don't count.

prompt: What is a coordination complex that carries an overall charge called?

choices.text: A complex ion
An organometallic compound
choices.why: That term is for complexes with metal–carbon bonds, whatever their charge.

choices.text: A double salt
choices.why: Double salts were the old name for combinations like AlF3·3KF. A charged coordination complex is a complex ion.

choices.text: A ligand
choices.why: Ligands are the Lewis bases bound to the metal, not the charged complex as a whole.

explanation: Coordination compounds are also called coordination complexes, metal complexes, or just complexes, and coordination complexes that are ions are called complex ions.

prompt: Which statement about organometallic compounds matches the section?

choices.text: They are complexes with metal–carbon bonds, and they are still a type of coordination compound
They are compounds with no metal–ligand coordinate bonds at all
choices.why: Organometallic compounds do have metal–ligand bonds; what sets them apart is that some bonds are to carbon.

choices.text: They are a class completely separate from coordination compounds
choices.why: The section stresses that organometallic compounds are just a type of coordination compound.

choices.text: They are any complexes containing organic counterions
choices.why: The defining feature is a metal–carbon bond in the primary coordination sphere, not organic counterions.

explanation: Complexes with metal–carbon bonds are called organometallic compounds. The distinction is convenient because many organometallic ligands do more than simple σ donation, but organometallic compounds are just a type of coordination compound, and some inorganic ligands behave similarly.

prompt: Why is the hexaamminecobalt(3+) ion written [Co(NH3)6]^3+ rather than [CoN6H18]^3+?

choices.text: Each ligand's atoms are kept together, so the formula shows the metal and its separate ligands
Because the hydrogen atoms are bonded directly to cobalt
choices.why: The H atoms are on nitrogen. Writing (NH3)6 shows six intact ammonia ligands, each bound through N.

choices.text: Because parentheses mark the outer coordination sphere
choices.why: Square brackets mark the primary sphere. Parentheses just keep a polyatomic ligand's atoms together.

choices.text: Because ammonia is a counterion
choices.why: The NH3 molecules are ligands inside the brackets, not counterions.

explanation: Formulas reflect the idea that a complex is a composite of metal and ligands. Ligand atoms aren't added to the rest of the compound; they're kept together, in parentheses or as an abbreviation. Square brackets enclose the primary coordination sphere.
